differences.label: Overall articulation rate faster than typical read speech
differences.text: Your articulation rate is 5.53 syllables per second of speech (pauses removed); read sentences average 3.40 (SD 0.42) across speakers (Jacewicz et al. 2009). Published norms differ with the method, so this is context only and costs no points.

differences.label: Pause longer than 1 s
differences.text: A 1.01 s pause after 'live'. In read speech, pauses over 1 s are rare (Campione & Veronis 2002); this is context only and costs no points.

flaws.context: sentence 2 of 4, middle of the sentence
flaws.fix: Let your pitch move about 5.2 st across these words, as it does elsewhere in your reading.
flaws.label: MONOTONE (recipe name)
flaws.measure: pitch range P90-P10 over the five-word window at the peak, st (your own typical range at this place in a sentence)
flaws.text: Narrower pitch range here than in the rest of your reading: 10.16-11.04 s ('I have up there that'). Your pitch range is 0.1 st here; at this place in a sentence your typical range is 5.2 st (1.3x the threshold; the ranges are compared as a ratio with 1 st added to each, flagged below x0.25). The span is approximate: this measure uses five-word windows. Costs 1.0 points of the delivery index relative to your own reading; score with this penalty removed: 96.6.
flaws.why: "if it's monotonous, your audience won't recall a word you said" (NSDA Declamation Starter Kit)

flaws.context: sentence 3 of 4, middle of the sentence
flaws.fix: Slow these words to about 1.7 s, in step with the rest of your reading.
flaws.label: RUSH (recipe name)
flaws.measure: speech time of the five-word window at the peak, s (expected time at your own typical pace)
flaws.text: Faster here than the rest of your reading: 15.80-17.14 s ('the Washington Monument, and then'). The word alignment measures 0.87 s of speech time in the five-word window at the peak; at your own typical pace these words take 1.70 s (expected from their length in sounds), 95% faster (1.4x the threshold; flagged beyond 62%). The span is approximate: this measure uses five-word windows. Costs 1.6 points of the delivery index relative to your own reading; score with this penalty removed: 97.2.
flaws.why: "If your speech is too fast paced, your audience won't catch a word you say." (NSDA Declamation Starter Kit)

flaws.context: sentence 4 of 4, middle of the sentence
flaws.fix: Keep these words at the level of the rest of your reading, about 15.3 dB louder.
flaws.label: FADE (recipe name)
flaws.measure: mean level over the five-word window at the peak, dB re your median voiced level
flaws.text: Quieter here than the rest of your reading: 22.00-24.02 s ('low, you can see past the Jefferson'). You are at -18.9 dB here relative to your median voiced level; your typical level is -3.6 dB, 15.3 dB higher (1.3x the threshold; flagged when 11.9 dB lower). The span is approximate: this measure uses five-word windows. Costs 1.8 points of the delivery index relative to your own reading; score with this penalty removed: 97.5.
flaws.why: "Every word you deliver should come across loud and clear to the audience." (NSDA Declamation Starter Kit)

notices: No second reading of the text: each stretch of this reading is compared with your own typical delivery over the same reading, corrected for what the text predicts there (the length of the words in sounds, the kind of boundary, the place in the sentence).
Emphasis, word time and endings are not measured in this mode: they need a second reading of the same text.

Flags are acoustic departures from your own typical delivery; pattern names describe the measured evidence, not a diagnosis. A delivery that is the same all through (for example fast everywhere) has no local departure and is not flagged. This mode finds fewer changes than a comparison with a second reading of the same text.
